title: The Set Contract & Mathematical Uniqueness
summary: Explore the Set interface: no duplicate elements, at most one null element (in HashSet), and mathematical set operations (union, intersection).
learningObjectives: Understand the formal mathematical contract of the java.util.Set interface
Master duplicate rejection mechanics and the boolean return value of add()
Contrast Set and List across indexing, uniqueness, and lookup performance
Analyze memory and time trade-offs between linear scanning and hashing
expectedOutcomes: Ability to determine precisely when business rules demand Set semantics over List
Mastery of conditional insertion patterns utilizing Set.add() return values

activities.title: Practical Context: Identity Rosters vs Sequential Activity Logs

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Identity Rosters vs Sequential Activity Logs
analogy.story:
In production architectures, datasets naturally divide into two distinct paradigms:

1. Sequential transaction streams: Every user action, click event, and payment log matters in the exact order it occurred, with duplicates expected and valid.
2. Identity registries: A registered user database, a system permission list, or an inventory of active IP addresses cannot tolerate duplicates. An identity either belongs to the system or it does not.

While Lists represent the former, Sets represent the mathematical reality of distinct identity registries.
analogy.keyTakeaway: A List preserves arrival order and tolerates duplicates. A Set models mathematical uniqueness: elements cannot duplicate, and membership lookups prioritize near-instant verification over sequential indexing.

activities.title: Understanding the Set Contract: Mathematical Sets in Java Collections

keyTakeaways: The java.util.Set interface prohibits duplicate elements according to equals()
The add(E e) method returns false if the element is already present, rejecting duplicates silently without throwing exceptions
Sets do not have index-based positional access (no get(int index) method)
Membership verification with contains() operates in O(1) time in HashSet compared to O(N) in List

activities.title: High-Speed Member De-Duplication and Ingestion
activities.description: Step through a realistic access control module verifying authorized user credentials while discarding duplicate logins.

steps.description: Instantiate a private final HashSet to guarantee O(1) membership lookups and prevent duplicate badges.
Validate input and invoke activeSecurityBadges.add(badgeId). The boolean return value immediately signals if the badge was newly issued or already registered.
Execute isBadgeActive() via contains(). In a hash set, this executes in constant O(1) average time without scanning the collection.
Main demonstrates attempting to issue SEC-001 twice. The second invocation cleanly evaluates to false, leaving set size at exactly 2.

questions.question: What occurs when set.add("Java") is executed on a HashSet that already contains the string "Java"?
options: An IllegalArgumentException is thrown at runtime
The method returns false and the existing element is retained without changes
The previous element is overwritten and the method returns true
questions.explanation: According to the java.util.Set contract, if an equal element already exists, the set leaves the collection unchanged and returns false.

questions.question: Why does the Set interface not provide a get(int index) method like List?
options: Because Java collections cannot store integers as indices
Because the Set contract models mathematical sets, which have no intrinsic positional or index-based ordering
Because Set extends Map which only uses keys
Because Java arrays cannot be converted into Sets
questions.explanation: Mathematical sets are defined strictly by membership, not sequential position. Since implementations like HashSet do not guarantee ordering, index-based access is intentionally excluded from the interface.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of set.contains(element) in a well-distributed HashSet versus list.contains(element) in an ArrayList?
questions.explanation: ArrayList must linearly scan up to N elements (O(N)), while HashSet calculates the hash bucket directly, delivering O(1) average lookup time.

questions.question: How many null elements can a java.util.HashSet hold?
options: Zero; null always throws NullPointerException in all Sets
Unlimited null elements as long as memory permits
Up to 16 null elements matching DEFAULT_INITIAL_CAPACITY
questions.explanation: HashSet permits null elements, but because Sets enforce uniqueness, at most one null reference can exist in the set.

questions.question: When should a software engineer choose a Set over a List in production systems?
questions.answer: Choose a Set when: 1) Business requirements strictly demand uniqueness (e.g., email registries, permission flags, foreign keys), 2) High-throughput membership checking via contains() is required (O(1) in HashSet vs O(N) in List), or 3) Mathematical set operations (union, intersection, difference) need to be evaluated across collections. Choose a List when arrival order must be preserved, duplicates are meaningful (e.g., financial ledger entries), or random positional access via index is necessary.

questions.question: How does Set.add() avoid race conditions or double-lookups in idiomatic Java?
questions.answer: Instead of writing defensive code like `if (!set.contains(item)) { set.add(item); }` (which performs two consecutive hash bucket traversals and is vulnerable to race conditions in concurrent contexts), idiomatic Java relies on the boolean return value of `set.add(item)`. The add() operation checks existence and inserts atomically in a single hash operation, returning true if added or false if already present.

questions.question: Can a custom object be stored in a Set if it only implements equals() but not hashCode()?
questions.answer: Technically Java allows it to compile, but it leads to critical runtime defects in HashSet and LinkedHashSet. If hashCode() is not overridden, the JVM uses default identity hash codes (derived from memory address). Two objects considered identical by equals() will produce different hash codes and land in different buckets, allowing duplicate objects into the set and breaking the fundamental Set contract.

activities.title: Self-Evaluation: Set Contract & Uniqueness
checklist: I can clearly define the Set contract and explain how duplicate rejection operates via equals() and hashCode()
I understand why Set omits index-based methods like get(int index) and how membership lookups achieve O(1) performance
I can leverage the boolean return value of Set.add() to streamline membership insertion logic

practiceProblems.title: Filter Duplicate IP Addresses
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given a list of IP address strings containing duplicates, implement a method that returns the total count of unique IP addresses using a Set.
hints: HashSet has a constructor that accepts any existing Collection: new HashSet<>(collection)
The size() method of the resulting set directly reflects the number of unique elements.

practiceProblems.title: Identify First Duplicate Element
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method that scans an array of numbers and returns the first number that appears more than once. If all numbers are distinct, return -1.
hints: Use seen.add(num). When add() returns false, you have encountered the first duplicate immediately.
This achieves O(N) time complexity and O(N) space, avoiding nested loops.

practiceProblems.title: Check If Array Has All Distinct Elements
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Write a method hasAllUnique(String[] tokens) that returns true if every token in the array is distinct, or false if any duplicate exists.
hints: Iterate through each item and check if set.add() succeeds.
Early return false as soon as any add() call returns false.

practiceProblems.title: Safe Bulk Registration Registry
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a RegistrationBook class with registerUser(String username) returning true if newly registered, and isRegistered(String username) checking existence in O(1) time.
hints: Normalize usernames with trim().toLowerCase() before adding or checking.
Delegate directly to set.add() and set.contains().

practiceProblems.title: Find Missing Numbers in Permutation
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given an integer array nums of length N containing numbers in the range [1, N+1], exactly one number is missing. Find and return the missing number using a Set.
hints: Insert all numbers into a HashSet in O(N) time.
Check which integer from 1 to N+1 is absent via set.contains(i) in O(1) time.
